newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries sharply down at midday after data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries sharply down at midday after data.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities were sharply lower at midday on Friday as strong employment and manufacturing reports took the wind out of the bond market's sails.

U.S. nonfarm payrolls rose by 316,000 in July, the government reported, against market expectations in the range of a rise of about 200,000. The unemployment rate also dropped to 4.8 percent, from 5.0 percent.
Midmorning, the National Association of Purchasing Management reported its July index rose to 58.6 percent from 55.7 in June.
Bond prices tumbled sharply following the NAPM release after having opened steady and fallen moderately after the release of payrolls an hour and a half earlier.

Economists at MMS International noted that the 0.3 percent decline in the average workweek contained in the report resulted in a 0.6 decline in the number of hours worked in July, despite the payrolls gain.
"This should leave the hours-worked index growing at only a 1.0 percent clip in the third quarter, which is consistent with GDP growth in the 2.0 percent area," they noted.
Despite this, traders said there was ample room for the market to vent out many of the recent gains it has recorded and a corrective movement was not unexpected.

"It's (the recert bond rally) over. The market has been discounting strong numbers, and relative to today's numbers the fall has been relatively muted," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co.

But eventually economic data will affect the market and the biggest problem currently was the lofty level the market has priced in -- more as if the Federal Reserve was in an easing phase rather tightening, Strauss said.
He said that with declines recently seen in yields on the 10-year Treasury issue, portfolio managers had been buying Treasuries with "reckless abandon."

In addition, Strauss said the market was at incredibly large levels going into supply next week. The Treasury will sell $16 billion of three-year notes on Tuesday; $12 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10 billion of 30-year bonds on Thursday in addition to its regular weekly auction of $17 billion of three- and six-month bills on Monday.
All the major numbers seen recently were indictive of a rapidly growing economy, Strauss said.
He said payrolls growth could not be ignored, even allowing for the creation of government jobs and seasonal factors.

"The labor force is no longer growing, it was less than 100,000 for the third straight month, Strauss said. "This presents a problem and the risk is that growth exceeds the 3.0 to 3.5 percent I had seen in the second half."
Trading volume was high, with GovPX reporting more than $65 billion being exchanged shortly after noon.
The Fed intervened in the money market via a round of weekend system repurchase agreements on Friday.
The Treasury's 30-year bond was trading down 1-27/32 at 102-15/32 to yield 6.44 percent.

The two-year note was down 8/32 at 100-even to yield 5.88 percent. The five-year note was off 22/32 at 99/23/32 to yield 6.07 percent, while the 10-year note was down 1-6/32 at 103-9/32 to yield 6.17 percent.
The three-month bill was up three basis points at 5.13 percent; the six-month bill up seven basis points at 5.18 percent and the year bill up nine basis points at 5.23 percent.
(( -- John P. Hughes, N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1663 ))
